parts.title: My Saturday job at the hairdresser's
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Every Saturday, I work at a hairdresser's near my school. I am sixteen, and it is my first real job. When I started, I thought that I would be cutting hair straight away, but in fact, I only washed it for the first two months.

My boss, Kinga, is very kind but also very strict. She says that a good hairdresser must listen before she cuts. "Customers always know what they want," she told me, "but sometimes they cannot explain it." She teaches me to ask questions and to look at their face and style.

The worst part of the job is standing for eight hours. My feet hurt so much that I soak them in warm water when I get home. The best part is hearing the stories of the customers. An old man once told me about his time as a sailor, and a girl cried with happiness when she saw her new haircut.

Last week, Kinga let me trim a boy's fringe for the first time. My hands were shaking, but he was delighted. Now I know that I want to be a hairdresser when I leave school.

options: She cut the hair of children

parts.title: A short history of hairstyles
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Hairstyles have always been a way of showing who we are. [1] In ancient Egypt, rich people wore wigs made from real hair, and they put sweet oils on them.

In the Middle Ages, women often covered their hair with scarves or hats. [2] It was considered polite for them to keep it hidden, except at home.

In the eighteenth century, hair became very tall and wide. [3] Some people even put little ships and flowers in their wigs, and went out for a ride in a coach with the roof open.

In the 1920s, many young women cut their hair short for the first time. [4] People said that it was very shocking, but the style soon became popular.

Today, there are no strict rules about hair. [5] You can wear it long, short, curly, straight, blue or even pink, and nobody will be surprised.
sentences: In Egypt, the hair of poor children was often shaved.
The styles were so large that people could hardly walk through doors.
Even thousands of years ago, hair was a matter of fashion.
In some countries, it took years to learn the skill.
Many people still go to the same hairdresser all their lives.
Men and women could choose from many different colours.
This was a rule that they were taught from a young age.
It was a sign of freedom and of a new kind of life.

gaps.explanation: Even thousands of years ago hair was a matter of fashion, which leads to the example from ancient Egypt.
The rule that women hid their hair was taught from a young age, and the next sentence says it was polite to keep it hidden.
The tall styles were so large that people hardly walked through doors, and the next sentence gives more examples.
Short hair was a sign of freedom, and the next sentence says people found it shocking.
Many different colours follows the idea of no rules and leads to the blue and pink examples.

parts.title: Looking after your hair
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Healthy hair does not need a lot of expensive products. The first rule is not [1] wash it too often. Most people only need to use shampoo two or three times a week. When you do wash it, use warm water, not hot, [2] hot water can make hair dry. Brush gently, starting from the ends and working up to the top, [3] this prevents pain and damage. Hair also needs good food. Eating plenty of fruit, vegetables and fish is good [4] it. If you use a hairdryer, hold it a little far from your head and do not use it [5] day. Finally, remember to get a trim every two or three months, even if you want your hair to grow long. It keeps the ends healthy, and your hair will look [6] better.

gaps.explanation: Not to wash it too often: an infinitive after the rule.
Warm not hot water, because hot water can make hair dry: reason.
Brush gently because this prevents pain and damage: reason.
Good for your hair: the adjective good takes for.
"Do not use it every day" means do not use it daily.
Much better means a lot better; the comparative is intensified.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to Kellan’s Barbers! Let me tell you about our prices this month. A full cut with a wash and a style is twenty-five pounds, and a beard shape costs twenty. But if you only need a quick trim to keep your hair tidy, it’s just fifteen pounds, and it takes about ten minutes. Last year the trim was eighteen, but we are trying to bring more people in. If you come before ten in the morning on a weekday, you also get a free coffee. You can book online or just walk in, but on Saturdays we are always busy, so I’d call first.

question.explanation: The full cut is twenty-five, the beard shape twenty and last year’s trim eighteen, but the trim now costs only fifteen pounds.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Thank you for calling Hair by Kemal. We can’t answer right now. If you want a cut, you can usually come in on the same day, because those take only half an hour. For a trim, calling two days before is also fine, and it helps you to get your favourite time. But colouring takes up to three hours, and we only have two colourists, so please call at least a week before your appointment. In December I’d say even earlier, because everybody wants a party hairstyle. Leave your name and number after the tone, and we’ll call you back.

parts.title: A talk about a hair salon
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to my salon. My name is Kinga, and I have been a hairdresser for thirty years. I started when I was eighteen, so now you can calculate my age. Before that I wanted to be a nurse, but I fainted the first time I saw blood. I opened this shop twelve years ago. It used to be a bakery, and you can still smell the bread sometimes, I swear. Many customers think it’s been ten years, because the time passes quickly, but it’s really twelve. Today there are six stylists here. We were four at the beginning, then eight at one point, but two left to start their own business, so six is a good number. They are friendly and very well trained, and I trust every one of them. Let’s talk about prices. A basic cut costs twenty pounds. A cut with a colour is sixty, and a full wedding style is eighty. Children under ten pay half price, and I think this is fair. Those between ten and fourteen pay the student price, which is fifteen pounds. Finally, a word about something special. We collect all the long hair that people cut off, and we send it to a charity in the north of England. They make wigs for people who lose their hair when they are ill. It could be for a child or for a patient in hospital. Last year we sent enough hair for forty wigs. Some people think we make hats or brushes, or that we throw it away, but no. If you want to give your hair, just ask your stylist to put it in a bag for you. Right, let’s go to the main room to meet the team.

gaps.explanation: She has been a hairdresser for thirty years; eighteen is only the age when she started.
Customers think ten years, but it is really twelve.

gaps.prompt: Number of stylists in the team: ___
gaps.explanation: There were four, then eight, but now there are six stylists.

gaps.prompt: The price of a basic cut: ___ pounds
gaps.explanation: A basic cut costs twenty pounds; a cut with colour is sixty and a wedding style eighty.
Children under ten pay half price; those between ten and fourteen pay fifteen pounds.

gaps.prompt: The salon sends hair to make ___
gaps.explanation: The hair goes to a charity that makes wigs, not hats or brushes.

parts.title: An interview with a hairdresser
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Kellan, you’ve been a barber for twenty years. What do you like most about the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People expect me to say the salary, and honestly it’s a decent job, but nobody gets rich. And the hours are long, I often finish at nine at night. No, what I love are the talks. People tell me about their holidays, their children, their problems. Sometimes I feel more like a friend than a barber.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What’s the strangest thing a customer has asked for?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Oh, there are a few. A man once wanted a very long beard shaped like a triangle, that took ages. Another asked for blue hair, which was fun. But the strangest was a picture of his dog, cut into the hair on the back of his head. I almost said no, but he showed me the photo and I did my best. He was so happy.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you do when a customer is unhappy?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: First, I listen. I never argue, even if I think the person is wrong. Then I ask what exactly they don’t like and try to fix it. Asking them to leave is never a good idea, and I wouldn’t bother my boss, because I am the boss. Most people are fine after ten minutes.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you stay up to date?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Magazines are nice, and I do read them every month, but fashions change faster than that. I tried working abroad for a few months once, but it’s not necessary. What really helps is workshops, I go to three or four a year, and videos online, which I watch at night with a cup of tea.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do young people need to become good barbers?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not a university degree, certainly. And experience abroad is a bonus, not a must. What I look for is patience, because learning takes years, and a real love of meeting people. If someone doesn’t enjoy talking, it’s a very hard job.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why would you like to start a school?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s my dream. I’m not thinking about money, a school isn’t a business that makes much. And I’d still keep my shop, I’m not tired of it. The reason is simple: a lot of people helped me when I started, and I want to pass on everything I’ve learned to the next generation.
